[doc: patterns/engine-overview]
# LuckyEngine systems overview

A brief map of what the engine is and how its pieces connect. Consult this when you're unsure which system handles a request.

## Data model

- Project - the folder the user is working in. Contains `Assets/` and scene/config files.
- Scene - a collection of entities. One active scene at a time. Edit-time and runtime modes.
- Entity - the unit of scene content. Has a UUID. Holds components.
- Component - a data fragment on an entity (Transform, StaticMesh, RigidBody, PointLight, Script, etc.). See `components/*` docs.
- Asset - a reusable resource on disk under `Assets/`: meshes (.hsmesh), materials (.hmaterial), scripts (.cs), prefabs (.hprefab), textures.

## Runtime vs edit mode

- Edit mode: scene is paused, user is authoring. Tools like `set_entity_property`, `add_component`, `create_game_object` run here.
- Play mode: scene is simulating. Physics steps, scripts run (`OnUpdate`), user can interact.
- The agent can't toggle play mode directly; the user presses Play in the editor.

## Scripting

- Scripts are C# classes inheriting from `Hazel.Entity`, stored in `Assets/Scripts/.../Source/*.cs`.
- Attach a script to an entity via `add_component Script` with `meshHandle = "<Namespace>.<ClassName>"`.
- After editing a `.cs` file, call `build_script_assembly` to compile. The editor hot-reloads.
- The full C# API is documented under `csharp-api/*`: Entity (lifecycle, components, events), Input, Physics, Scene, Vector3, Prefab, Mathf.
- For robotics tasks (driving an arm to a Cartesian target, gripper control, pick-and-place), start at `patterns/robot-control` - the motion-graph + IK idiom is a different shape from generic scripting.

## Physics (Jolt)

- A `RigidBodyComponent` + a collider (`BoxCollider`, `SphereCollider`, `CapsuleCollider`, `MeshCollider`) make an entity physics-simulated.
- `BodyType`: `Static` (doesn't move), `Dynamic` (gravity + collisions), `Kinematic` (moved by code, pushes dynamics).
- See `components/RigidBody` for properties; `patterns/spawning` for dynamic spawning with gravity.

## Rendering

- Meshes come from `StaticMeshComponent`. They reference a mesh asset (`StaticMesh Handle`) and one or more material handles (slot 0, 1, ...). See `components/Material`.
- Lights: `DirectionalLight` (sun), `PointLight`, `SpotLight`, `SkyLight` (environment/ambient). See their individual docs.
- Camera: `CameraComponent` with `Primary=true` is the active view.

## Prefabs

- A prefab is a reusable entity template saved as `.hprefab`. Build one with `create_prefab_from_entity` or `create_game_object savePrefab="Name"`.
- At runtime, scripts `Instantiate(prefab, position, rotation)` to spawn clones. See `csharp-api/Prefab` and `patterns/spawning`.

## Tool landscape (what's available to the agent)

- Queries (safe, free): `search_entities`, `get_entity_properties`, `search_assets`, `get_current_scene`, `capture_viewport_screenshot`, `capture_scene`, `read_file`, `read_doc`, `search_docs`
- State-changing (require approval unless Auto-run is on): `create_entity`, `create_game_object`, `duplicate_entity`, `add_component`, `make_mujoco_dynamic_body`, `remove_component`, `set_entity_property`, `destroy_entity`, `batch_set_entity_property`, `batch_destroy_entities`, `create_material`, `create_prefab_from_entity`, `create_scene`, `open_scene`, `create_script`, `build_script_assembly`, `write_file`

## Preferred patterns by request type

| User wants... | Reach for |
|---|---|
| New scene from scratch | `patterns/scene-setup` |
| Falling/spawning things at runtime | `patterns/spawning` + `csharp-api/Prefab` |
| N similar entities, no robot interaction (decorative grid of cubes, row of static pillars, scattered props) | `patterns/bulk-authoring` - template -> `duplicate_entity` -> `batch_set_entity_property`. Not a loop of `create_game_object`. |
| Timed / periodic behavior ("every N seconds") | `patterns/timed-behaviors` + `csharp-api/Timer` |
| Any scripting task | `patterns/scripting-workflow` - end-to-end checklist (write -> build -> attach -> assign -> Play) |
| Script has tunables (numbers / bools / colors) you want editable from the inspector | `patterns/inspector-attributes` - `[Group]`/`[Tooltip]`/`[Slider]`/`[Units]`/`[ToggleButton]`/`[Dropdown]`/`[Button]`. Promote `const` -> `public` + attributes. |
| A camera that sees X | `create_entity` + `add_component Camera` + orientation |
| Separate lights and meshes | `patterns/entity-composition` |
| Non-mesh object (light, camera, script-host) | `patterns/non-visual-entities` |
| Color/material change on a mesh | `create_material` + assign to `Material 0` slot |
| Game behavior (input, movement, AI) | `patterns/scripting-workflow` first, then `csharp-api/Entity` |
| Drive a robot arm to a target / gripper control / discover graph inputs | `patterns/robot-control` |
| **Humanoid (G1) — walk / pick up a cup / locomotion + arm manipulation** ("make the G1 walk over here," "G1 picks up the cup," "walk to the table and grab it") | **`patterns/humanoid-policy-control`** — ships two calibrated templates: `HumanoidWalkDriver` (locomotion only) and `HumanoidPickPlaceDriver` (walk-up + arm-IK grasp). Use the template; don't hand-roll the joint masks / policy plumbing. Read first whenever the robot is a humanoid. |
| **Robot + objects scene** ("make a jenga scene with Piper", "Piper stacks blocks", "scene where the arm builds a tower / brick wall", "pick-and-place demo", anything pairing an arm robot with manipulable objects) | **`patterns/pick-and-place`** — the FULL recipe: authors the blocks (delegates to `bulk-authoring`) AND writes the pick-and-place controller script that drives the robot. "Make a jenga scene with Piper" means BOTH a Jenga stack AND a Piper that builds it — don't stop after placing static blocks. |
| **An object a MuJoCo robot should touch** (a cup to grasp, a table to rest it on, a ball to push) | **`patterns/mujoco-objects`** — `make_mujoco_dynamic_body` (dynamic vs static); a Jolt body won't collide with a MuJoCo robot. |
| Read or modify existing scripts | `search_assets assetType=ScriptFile` → `read_file` → `write_file` → follow `patterns/scripting-workflow` for build/attach |

## Core defaults (apply unless the user says otherwise)

- Query directly with `search_entities` filters; don't enumerate the scene first. "Make all lights red" -> `search_entities(hasAnyComponents=["PointLight","SpotLight","DirectionalLight","SkyLight"])` -> `batch_set_entity_property`. `search_entities()` with no filter as a discovery step wastes turns and context.
- For the same op on N entities, use `batch_set_entity_property` or `batch_destroy_entities`.
- For N similar entities at edit time, configure one template (with all its components), `duplicate_entity count=N`, then `batch_set_entity_property` to position them - see `patterns/bulk-authoring`. Don't loop `create_game_object`.
- To fix entities at wrong positions/sizes/colors, mutate with `set_entity_property` or `batch_set_entity_property` - don't destroy and recreate.
- Issue multiple tool calls in one response when they're independent - faster.
- When a user request mentions multiple roles (camera, lights, mesh, script), create a separate entity per role. See `patterns/entity-composition`.
- After non-trivial placement or scripting, verify with `capture_viewport_screenshot`.
- Don't modify files or entities unrelated to the user's request. Pre-existing errors in files you haven't touched are not your problem to fix.

## Be efficient with reads

Reading everything before acting exhausts the context budget and often leaves no room for the actual work. Rules of thumb:

- Pick a filtered `search_entities` call that already narrows to what you want - don't do an unfiltered overview pass first.
- Only `get_entity_properties` on the one entity you're about to modify.
- Only `read_doc` a topic when you can't remember a specific detail - don't read the whole doc tree.
- Don't re-read the same file; results are in your context from earlier in the turn.


[doc: patterns/humanoid-policy-control]
# Pattern: Humanoid (G1) — walk & pick up — at a glance

For any task with a **humanoid robot** (Unitree G1, bipeds) where locomotion is RL-policy driven and the arms are Cartesian-IK driven:

- *"Make the G1 walk over there."* → locomotion only.
- *"Make the G1 pick up the cup"* / *"walk to the table and grab the cup."* → locomotion + arm-IK grasp.

This doc is the **map**, not the implementation. Two calibrated script templates ship for it — **use them, don't re-derive**. Every brittle re-implementation of humanoid control has come from hand-rolling the joint masks, the policy plumbing, or the carry-pose math instead of starting from the template.

| Template (`create_script templateName=...`) | Use for |
|---|---|
| **`HumanoidWalkDriver`** | "walk to X", "go over there", "turn to face X" — locomotion only. Dead simple, reliable. |
| **`HumanoidPickPlaceDriver`** | "pick up the cup", "walk to the table and grab it" — locomotion + one-arm IK grasp + lift. |

If the robot is a stationary **arm** (Piper, Panda, SO100) — no legs, no walking — you want `patterns/pick-and-place`, not this doc.

---

## The whole job, in steps

### "Make the G1 walk to X"

1. `create_script scriptName="<Name>" templateName="HumanoidWalkDriver"`
2. `build_script_assembly`
3. `add_component entityID=<robot> componentType=Script meshHandle="<namespace>.<Name>"`
4. Assign the script's `WalkTarget` to the entity to walk toward (a marker, a table, anything).
5. Tell the user to press Play.

That's it — the template turns in place to face the target (rotator policy, falling back to the walker if none), then activates the walker and steers it there. No arm IK, no joint masks.

### "Make the G1 pick up the cup from the table"

1. **Scene** — if there's no cup/table yet, author them as **MuJoCo** bodies (a Jolt cup won't collide with the robot). Cup = dynamic, table = static. Recipe in `patterns/mujoco-objects`. Place the cup near the table edge facing the robot.
2. **Controller** — `create_script scriptName="<Name>" templateName="HumanoidPickPlaceDriver"`, then `build_script_assembly`, then `add_component ... meshHandle="<namespace>.<Name>"`.
3. **Wire it** — assign `TargetObject` = the cup. Optionally assign `StandTarget` = a marker in front of the table so the body parks clear of the furniture.
4. **Create a draggable grasp marker** (recommended). Make a small empty entity at the cup's grasp point (`create_entity` near the cup, e.g. the cup's XYZ) and assign it to the controller's `GraspTarget`. The hand then aims its grasp_site exactly at that marker, so the user can **drag it in the editor to guide the hand onto the cup** instead of editing offset numbers. (Leave `GraspTarget` null to auto-derive the grasp point from the cup.)
5. **Set the robot-specific names** (see §2): the **IK input names** and **finger actuator names** to match this robot.
6. Tell the user to press Play — and that the grasp orientation will likely need a Play-time tune (drag `GraspTarget` to fix position; tune `GraspOrientationEuler` to fix the wrist angle).

The template runs the phase machine: `Startup → FaceTurn → WalkTo → Settle → Draw → Extend → Descend → Seat → Close → Lift → Done`. It **turns in place to face the target first** (rotator), walks up, then frees the active arm and reaches with a **"western-draw" arc** — raise the hand UP (Draw), push FORWARD over the table staying high (Extend), come straight DOWN onto the object (Descend). The Draw/Extend/Descend approach is **position-only** so the hand reliably reaches the cup; orientation is then enforced in the **Seat** phase, which re-sends the *same* grasp position with `Solve_Orientation` on so the wrist rotates to the grasp angle **in place** (a wrist-only solve — far more reachable than orienting mid-approach). The policy keeps the legs/waist/off-arm balancing throughout.

> **Facing requires the rotator policy.** The clean turn-in-place uses the **rotator** (slot 2) — the walker fights pure-yaw commands and shuffles. If the robot has no rotator registered, the template falls back to turning with the walker (works, but less clean). For a robot to expose a rotator, its pack must ship `policy_descriptor.rotator.json` + the rotator model and register it in `PolicyRegistry.yaml` with a policy slot. The inspire-hand `UnitreeG1` ships this (plus a `croucher`); some G1 packs (e.g. the Five-Fingers build) historically shipped only the walker — confirm via `get_entity_properties → Policy Slots`.

---

## §2. IK input names — DISCOVER them, never assume (the #1 cause of "nothing happens")

The motion-graph input identifiers are **graph-asset-specific and differ between G1 builds.** The template defaults to one convention; if your robot uses the other, the arm silently won't move. **Always** read the real names first:

```
get_entity_properties <robotEntityID>
→ RobotControllerComponent → Exposed Inputs lists the exact identifiers
```

Two conventions seen in the wild:

| Concept | "Five Fingers" G1 (`MG_UnitreeG1FiveFingers`) — template default | CupCleaner inspire-hand G1 |
|---|---|---|
| Arm target position | `LeftArm_Target_Position` / `RightArm_Target_Position` | `Left_Target` / `Right_Target` |
| Arm target orientation | `LeftArm_Target_Orientation` | `Left_Target_Orientation` |
| Elbow pole target | `LeftArm_Pole_Target` | `Left_Pole_Target` |
| Elbow pole weight | `LeftArm_Pole_Weight` | `Left_Pole_Weight` |

Set the template's `IK Input Names` group to whatever `get_entity_properties` actually shows. **Position is metres (world), orientation is degrees (Euler XYZ)** at the input boundary.

Same discovery applies to the **finger actuators**: the template's `FingerActuatorNames` default is the CupCleaner inspire-hand set; a different hand has different actuator names. Read them from the robot's MJCF or the actuator list.

---

## §3. Scene layout

- **Cup / object** — dynamic MuJoCo body with a **mesh collider** (`make_mujoco_dynamic_body shape="mesh"`) — a `cylinder` primitive collider is too slippery to grasp. See `patterns/mujoco-objects`.
- **Table / fixture** — static MuJoCo body with a **box collider** (`make_mujoco_dynamic_body shape="box" isStatic=true`; a box is fine for a box), **~0.74 m tall** so the cup sits at the standing G1's arm height (a knee-high table is unreachable).
- **Where** — within reach of the standing robot. Put the table ~1 m out and the cup on the near edge. The `HumanoidPickPlaceDriver` walks to `StandDistance` (default **0.42 m** — the G1's forward arm reach) from the `StandTarget` (or the object), then reaches. **If the hand stops short of the cup, lower `StandDistance`; if the body bumps the table, raise it** — this is the main tuning knob. Sit the cup slightly above the tabletop so it settles on Play.
- **A stand marker is worth it** when the cup is in the middle of a table — point `StandTarget` at an empty spot in front of the table so the body doesn't try to walk into the table to reach the cup.

---

## §4. Mental model — three stacked control surfaces (why the template does what it does)

A G1 has ONE `RobotControllerComponent` owning three concurrent surfaces:

- **Policies (RL networks)** — `walker` (slot 1), `rotator` (slot 2), sometimes `croucher`/`reacher` (scene-scoped). Activated independently; each can drive a **subset** of joints (its driven-joints mask). Commanded via `SetFloat(slotId, commandId, value)`.
- **Motion-graph IK** — the per-arm `*_Target` inputs drive a LimbIK solver for the shoulder/elbow/wrist chain, **but only for joints not claimed by an active policy**.
- **Joint ownership** — `SetDrivenJoints(slotId, jointNames[])` declares which joints a policy may write.

**The invariant the template upholds:** every joint has **exactly one** owner per frame. Either an active policy claims it, or IK drives it, or the script writes the actuator. Two owners = fighting = jitter. Zero owners = the joint sags.

The "active arm on IK, everything else on policy" trick = set the walker's mask to *everything except the active arm's 7 joints*. The template bakes both masks in:

```
left-hand grasp  → walker mask = legs + waist + RIGHT arm   (left arm free for IK)
right-hand grasp → walker mask = legs + waist + LEFT arm    (right arm free for IK)
```

Walker command ids (1-based, descriptor order): `1=SetVx` (m/s fwd), `2=SetVy` (m/s strafe, usually 0), `3=SetYawRate` (rad/s). Same ids for the rotator.

---

## §5. Calibrated constants (baked into the templates — skim, don't re-derive)

| Constant | Template default | Note |
|---|---|---|
| Walk speed | 0.5 m/s | walker trained around this |
| Stand distance | 0.42 m | body parks this far from the object — must be ≤ the arm's forward reach (~0.5 m). The knob to tune if the hand stops short. |
| Yaw gain / max yaw rate | 2.0 / 1.0 rad/s | heading P-controller; cap keeps the walker stable |
| Approach back-off | 0.25 m | pre-grasp hover sits this far back along body→object |
| Pre-grasp lift | 0.12 m | hover this high, then descend onto the object |
| Reach-through | 0.05 m | push past the grasp point so fingers wrap around it |
| Pole weight | 1.0 | elbow-hint fully respected during reach + carry |
| Settle / approach dwell | 0.6 s / 0.6 s | let the body and IK chain settle before moving |
| Carry pose | fwd 0.30, up 0.45, lateral 0.12 m (pelvis-relative) | tracks the body's live yaw each frame |

**Wrist orientation is enforced (`SolveOrientation = true`) but applied position-safely.** The approach (Draw/Extend/Descend) runs with orientation OFF so the hand reliably reaches the cup; the **Seat** phase then turns orientation on and re-sends the same position, rotating the wrist in place. `GraspOrientationEuler` is a body-local offset — `.X` = pitch from the ground (default **-90**), `.Y` is added to the body's facing yaw (tracks whichever way the robot turned), `.Z` = roll.

**The exact orientation Euler is robot-specific — you WILL tune it in Play.** It depends on the robot's `grasp_site` frame: the Five-Fingers `left_grasp_site` carries `quat="0.707107 0 0.707107 0"` (a 90° rotation about Y), whereas CupCleaner's `left_palm_site` is identity — so the same Euler means different physical poses on the two robots, and CupCleaner's values do NOT transfer. Because the Seat phase reaches position first, a wrong Euler only twists the wrist in place (the hand still arrives at the cup), so it's easy to dial: nudge `GraspOrientationEuler` until the palm seats. The other robot-specific knobs: the IK/finger names from §2.

---

## §6. Policy switching protocol (only if you change policies — `HumanoidWalkDriver` doesn't)

When swapping between locomotion policies (walker → rotator for a clean turn-in-place, walker → croucher to drop height):

1. **Zero the outgoing policy's commands** (`SetVx=0, SetYawRate=0`) *before* deactivating it — an inactive slot keeps stale commands.
2. `SetPolicyActive(outgoing, false)`.
3. `SetPolicyActive(incoming, true)`.
4. `SetDrivenJoints(incoming, mask)` — apply the SAME arm-exclusion mask to the incoming policy if an arm is on IK; otherwise it'll reclaim the arm on activation.
5. Set the incoming policy's initial commands.

Special cases:
- **Walker → Rotator (turn in place):** settle the walker (`vx=0, yawRate=0`) for ~0.5 s first so the body is at a standstill; the rotator was trained to turn from rest and stumbles if it inherits forward momentum. Ramp the rotator's yaw command in over ~0.5 s to avoid a lurch.
- **Near-180° turns** sit where shortest-path yaw flip-flops — force a direction rather than trusting the sign of the error.
- **`freeze_joints` in a descriptor** snap those joints to `default_pos` the instant the policy activates, erasing IK's work — activate the policy *before* the IK chain poses the arm.

---

## §7. Failure modes

| Symptom | Cause | Fix |
|---|---|---|
| Arm doesn't move at all during the grasp | IK input names don't match the robot's graph. | §2 — `get_entity_properties`, set the `IK Input Names` fields. |
| **Only the fingers close — the arm never reaches** | The arm IK never got triggered. This G1 graph is **trigger-based**: it interpolates the grasp_site to the target over `Duration` only when the `Start` trigger fires — writing `*_Target_Position` every frame with no trigger does nothing. The fingers move because they're driven directly via actuators, bypassing the graph. | The template fires `Start` once per IK move (`SendArmMove` → set target/orientation/pole/`Duration`, then `SetInputTrigger(Start)`). Confirm the `DurationInput`/`StartInput` names match the graph. (Some graphs are continuous-tracking instead — like CupCleaner's — and need no trigger; this one isn't.) |
| **Fingers half-close / curl unevenly / "each finger moves on its own"** | Finger joints driven at hardcoded angles that don't match this hand's joint ranges, so some clamp and some fall short. | The template drives all 12 finger joints from ONE close scalar (0→1), mapping it onto **each joint's own actuator ctrlrange** (`GetActuatorCtrlRange`) — so the whole hand closes together, correctly, on any hand. Confirm the joint names exist in the robot's MJCF. |
| Robot stands rigid, never walks | Walker not active, or `SetVx` never written (defaults to 0). | Template activates it in `OnCreate` and writes commands every frame — confirm `WalkerSlotId` matches the robot's walker slot. |
| Robot walks but veers / never turns | Heading control missing or `WalkerSlotId` wrong. | Template writes `SetYawRate` each frame; verify the slot id. |
| Robot arcs toward the target / sets off facing the wrong way | Steering with the walker alone from a large initial heading error, with no turn-in-place first. | `TurnToFaceFirst` (default on) turns in place before walking; for a clean turn the robot needs a **rotator** policy (slot 2) registered — otherwise it falls back to a walker shuffle. |
| Arm twitches / fights the body | Active-arm joints claimed by BOTH walker and IK. | Template excludes the active arm via `SetDrivenJoints` at the handoff — don't widen the mask. |
| Fingers close but the cup isn't held / slips through | `FingerActuatorNames` wrong, or open/close values/sign wrong for this hand. | §2 — set the finger actuator names; confirm `GripCloseValue` direction from the MJCF. |
| **Hand stuck up in the air, grasping at nothing** | Orientation was enforced *during* the approach with an Euler that's infeasible at the low cup pose, so the IK couldn't reach down. | The approach is now position-only; orientation is seated in place at the cup (Seat phase). If you still see it high, the approach (Draw/Extend/Descend) shouldn't have orientation on — confirm `SolveOrientation` is only applied at Seat. |
| Hand reaches the cup but the wrist isn't at 90° from ground | `GraspOrientationEuler` not yet tuned for this robot's `grasp_site` frame. | Tune `GraspOrientationEuler` in Play (`.X` pitch-from-ground, `.Y` yaw offset added to facing, `.Z` roll). The hand stays on the cup while you adjust (Seat is a wrist-only solve), so iterate until the palm seats. |
| Hand is *close* but a few degrees / cm off (e.g. 87° not 90°, slightly high) | The IK is at its solver-accuracy / reach-envelope limit and compromises position vs orientation. | `HighAccuracy` (on by default) tightens the solver. Beyond that, give the arm margin: lower `StandDistance` so the body is closer (less arm extension), and drag `GraspTarget` to the exact spot. Sub-degree precision on a generic blind template is genuinely hard — this is manual-tune territory. |
| Elbow flips into a "chicken wing" | Pole hint off or weak. | Template writes `*_Pole_Target` + `Pole_Weight=1.0`; tune `PoleOffset` if needed. |
| Cup-in-hand drifts off as the body moves | Carry target is world-pinned, not body-relative. | Template recomputes the carry pose from live pelvis each frame — don't replace it with a fixed point. |
| `SetFloat(slot, …)` does nothing | Wrong slot id, or policy inactive. | Confirm slot from `get_entity_properties` Policy Slots; the scene's generated `<Scene>PolicyIds` enum carries scene-scoped ids. |

---

## §8. Beyond a single pickup (advanced)

The `HumanoidPickPlaceDriver` covers walk-up + grasp + lift. For full multi-step cycles — carry to a bin, drop, switch hands, repeat, bimanual — the CupCleaner project uses an orchestrator + per-phase subroutine architecture (its current controller is `GrabUpDownTurnTasksV2`, a ~140-line composition over a shared subroutine library). That's overkill for a single pickup; reach for it only when you have >5 branching phases, multiple robots sharing a task surface, or interruptible/resumable cycles. If the user has that project open and names its path, `read_file` the relevant subroutine; otherwise the two templates here are the supported, self-contained path.

---

## §9. Pre-Play checklist

- [ ] Controller generated via `create_script templateName="HumanoidWalkDriver"` or `"HumanoidPickPlaceDriver"`, NOT written from scratch.
- [ ] `get_entity_properties` run on the robot; `IK Input Names` and `FingerActuatorNames` set to match (pickup only).
- [ ] `WalkerSlotId` / `PelvisBodyName` confirmed against the robot.
- [ ] Cup is a **dynamic** MuJoCo body, table is **static** — per `patterns/mujoco-objects`. No Jolt bodies in a MuJoCo scene.
- [ ] `TargetObject` (and `StandTarget` if used) assigned; object is within reach after the walk.
- [ ] Script built (`build_script_assembly`) and attached (`add_component Script meshHandle="<namespace>.<Name>"`).
- [ ] Summary tells the user to press Play AND that grasp orientation / carry pose may need a Play-time tuning pass.

See also: `patterns/mujoco-objects` (authoring the cup + table), `patterns/robot-control` (motion-graph + IK + actuator contract), `patterns/pick-and-place` (stationary-arm manipulation tricks that also apply once an arm is IK-driven), `patterns/scripting-workflow`, `patterns/inspector-attributes`.

# Pattern: Authoring MuJoCo objects (cups, tables, blocks, props)

When the scene contains a MuJoCo robot (Piper, Unitree G1, any robot with a `MujocoScene` component or a `Mujoco*Collider` already present), **every object the robot should touch must live in the MuJoCo physics world** — not Jolt. The two physics worlds are disjoint: a Jolt rigid body will never collide with a MuJoCo robot, so a cup made with a Jolt `RigidBody` + `BoxCollider` will fall straight through the robot's hand.

This doc is the recipe for authoring those objects. Read it whenever you're adding a graspable/pushable object, a table or fixture, or a pile of blocks to a robot scene.

---

## The one tool you need: `make_mujoco_dynamic_body`

**This tool exists.** It is in your schema (state-changing tools, requires approval unless Auto-run is on). If a pattern doc references it, call it — do not assume it's missing and improvise a Jolt body or a manual collider+joint pair.

```
make_mujoco_dynamic_body  entityID=<UUID>  shape="box"            ← dynamic (collider + free joint, 6 DOF)
make_mujoco_dynamic_body  entityID=<UUID>  shape="cylinder"  isStatic=false
make_mujoco_dynamic_body  entityID=<UUID>  shape="box"  isStatic=true  ← static (collider only, welded to world)
```

What it does in one call:
- **`isStatic=false` (default)** — adds the matching `Mujoco<Shape>Collider` **and** a `MujocoJoint` of type `free`. The free joint is what gives the body its 6 degrees of freedom — there is no "MujocoRigidBody" component; this is the MuJoCo idiom. Use for anything the robot picks up, pushes, or knocks over (cups, blocks, balls).
- **`isStatic=true`** — adds only the collider, welded to the world. Use for fixtures the robot rests things on or against (tables, shelves, walls, the bin in a cleanup task).

`shape` accepts `box`, `sphere`, `capsule`, `cylinder`, or `mesh` (wrap an existing StaticMesh on the entity). The collider **size comes from the entity's scale**, so set the scale on `create_game_object` first.

---

## Recipe: a graspable cup on a table

```
# (1) Table — a static MuJoCo fixture the cup rests on.
create_game_object  name="Table"  shape="Cube"
  x=0.0  y=0.37  z=1.0                  ← ~1 m out in front so the robot has a clear walk-up
  scaleX=0.6  scaleY=0.74  scaleZ=0.4   ← ~0.74 m tall (waist/low-chest); TOP surface = y + scaleY/2 = 0.74.
  colorR=0.45 colorG=0.30 colorB=0.18      A thin floating tabletop (scaleY=0.05) sits at knee height — too low to reach.
  addCollider=false                     ← never the Jolt shortcut in a MuJoCo scene
make_mujoco_dynamic_body  entityID=<Table>  shape="box"  isStatic=true   ← box primitive collider (static) — a box is fine for a box

# (2) Cup — a small dynamic MuJoCo cylinder on the NEAR (robot-facing) edge of the tabletop.
create_game_object  name="Cup"  shape="Cylinder"
  x=0.0  y=0.78  z=0.85                 ← near edge (table front ≈ z 0.8), top 0.74 + cup half-height; reachable after walk-up
  scaleX=0.05  scaleY=0.05  scaleZ=0.05
  colorR=0.85 colorG=0.15 colorB=0.12
  addCollider=false
make_mujoco_dynamic_body  entityID=<Cup>  shape="mesh"   ← MESH collider, NOT "cylinder"
```

Two tool calls per object. The cup is now a 6-DOF MuJoCo body the robot's hand can actually grasp and lift.

**Match the collider to the shape: graspable ROUND objects use `mesh`; boxes/flat surfaces use the `box` primitive.**
- **Cup (and other graspable round objects — bottles, cans):** use `shape="mesh"`. The `cylinder`/`sphere` primitive presents a smooth round side the fingers slide off, so the grasp won't hold; the mesh's faceted convex hull gives stable multi-point finger contact.
- **Table / box fixtures:** use `shape="box"`. A box collider is exact for a box — no reason to mesh-decompose it.

**Table height — make it tall enough to reach.** A standing G1's arms work comfortably around **0.7–0.8 m** (waist to low chest). A thin tabletop at `y=0.4` puts the surface near the knees, below the arm's natural workspace — the IK then has to reach down awkwardly or can't reach at all. Build the table as a solid box from the floor (`scaleY ≈ 0.74`) or float a top at `y ≈ 0.74`.

**Placement rule — keep it in reach.** The object only matters if the robot can reach it. For a stationary arm, that's the arm's reach envelope (see `patterns/pick-and-place §3` for the Piper). For a humanoid that walks up to a table: put the table **~1 m out** for a clear walk-up and the cup on the **near (robot-facing) edge**. The `HumanoidPickPlaceDriver` stops ~`StandDistance` (default 0.42 m — the G1's forward arm reach) short of the cup, then reaches; so the near-edge cup lands inside the arm's envelope. If the hand stops short on Play, lower `StandDistance`; if the body bumps the table, raise it. Sit objects slightly **above** their rest surface so they settle onto it on Play rather than starting interpenetrating (MuJoCo ejects overlapping bodies).

---

## Many similar objects (a pile of blocks)

For N similar dynamic bodies, **configure ONE template, then duplicate** — don't loop `create_game_object` + `make_mujoco_dynamic_body` N times. Add the MuJoCo body to the template first; `duplicate_entity` deep-copies the collider + free joint onto every clone. Full recipe in `patterns/bulk-authoring`; stacking geometry in `patterns/pick-and-place`.

---

## Static vs dynamic — pick correctly

| Object | Static or dynamic | Why |
|---|---|---|
| Cup, block, ball, anything grasped/pushed | **dynamic** (`isStatic=false`) | needs 6 DOF to be moved by the robot |
| Table, shelf, wall, floor, bin shell | **static** (`isStatic=true`) | a fixture; must not drift when bumped |
| The robot itself | neither | already a `MujocoScene` — don't add colliders to it |

If a "static" fixture is given a free joint it will slowly drift or get shoved across the floor when the robot leans on it. If a "dynamic" object is left static it'll be immovable and the grasp looks like it's glued. Getting this wrong is the most common MuJoCo-authoring mistake.

---

## What NOT to do

- **Don't use `addCollider=true` on `create_game_object`** in a MuJoCo scene — that adds the **Jolt** collider, which the MuJoCo robot can't see.
- **Don't add `RigidBody` + `BoxCollider`/`SphereCollider`** (those are Jolt). Use `make_mujoco_dynamic_body`.
- **Don't try to "weld the cup to the hand"** to fake a grasp. `MujocoSceneComponent.WeldBody` pins a body to the **world**, not to another body — it can't make a cup ride along with a moving hand. Grasp via the gripper/fingers closing on the object (friction), as the controller templates do.
- **Don't teleport a MuJoCo body** by writing its `Transform.Translation` in a script — MuJoCo owns its pose each step and overwrites you. Move it with forces or, for resets, `WeldBody`.

---

See also: `patterns/pick-and-place` (arm + objects: block geometry, reach envelope), `patterns/humanoid-policy-control` (G1 + objects: walk-up + grasp), `patterns/bulk-authoring` (N similar objects), `patterns/robot-control` (the motion-graph/actuator side).

# Pattern: Driving a robot via motion graph + IK

Driving a robot arm to a Cartesian target is done by feeding named inputs into a `RobotControllerComponent`, which routes them through a motion-graph asset (`.hmograph`) containing IK nodes. The script never poses joints directly - it sets target position/orientation/duration, fires a trigger, and the graph + IK solver does the rest. Grippers (and any non-IK degrees of freedom) are MuJoCo actuators, not graph inputs.

Use this any time the user wants Cartesian-space robot motion: moving an end-effector to a pose, sequencing multi-step manipulation, opening/closing a gripper.

For pick-and-place / stacking / Jenga / brick walls / "move block A onto block B" tasks, also read `patterns/pick-and-place` - it builds on this doc with the manipulation tricks (lift-then-translate, gripper yaw canonicalization, hover-drop, layer cascade), a self-contained `ArmDriver` skeleton, and slot geometry for the common stack shapes.

**For humanoid robots (Unitree G1, bipeds) - walking, turning, crouching, locomotion + manipulation - read `patterns/humanoid-policy-control` instead** (or in addition to). Humanoids layer an RL-policy locomotion controller (walker / rotator / croucher) on top of the arm IK described here; the trick is managing which joints belong to the policy vs. IK on each frame via `SetDrivenJoints`. This doc covers the arm-IK plumbing; humanoid-policy-control covers the policy plumbing and the policy<->IK handoff.

## Anti-patterns - what NOT to do

Common mistakes that look plausible but break under MuJoCo:

- **Don't write `entity.Translation` / `entity.Rotation` on the robot's link entities.** MuJoCo owns those each Physics tick - the solver overwrites your write on the next step. The arm will appear frozen or jitter.
- **Don't teleport physics-owned objects** by setting their `Translation` in `OnUpdate`. If the object has a rigid body or a free joint, MuJoCo owns its pose; direct transform writes are either ignored or break contact/collision. Move objects by applying forces, setting joint state, or - for kinematic resets - `MujocoSceneComponent.WeldBody`.
- **Don't author a hand-rolled trajectory in `OnUpdate`** by lerping link rotations frame-by-frame. The graph already does this for you, accurately, with IK.
- **Don't try to drive the arm by writing to MuJoCo joint qpos directly.** Joint state is *readable* from script but not *writable* - see "Fallback" below for the correct lower-level path.

## 1. Discover the controller and its inputs

```
get_entity_properties <robot-root-entity-id>
```

Expect a `RobotControllerComponent` and a `MujocoSceneComponent` on the robot root entity. The entity-properties listing should also surface the attached motion graph's exposed inputs - names and types. If it doesn't, treat one of these as the source of truth:

- Ask the user for the input identifier names.
- Open the `.hmograph` asset and read the input port list.
- Read an existing script that already drives this robot to see which input names its graph exposes.

**Input names are graph-asset-specific.** Don't hardcode them from memory; discover them per-scene.

## 2. Identifiers - use the string constructor

Inputs are addressed by `Hazel.Identifier`. The constructor you want is:

```csharp
private static readonly Identifier TargetPositionID = new Identifier("TargetPosition");
```

If `inspect_script_api("Hazel.Identifier")` only shows `Identifier.FromId(uint)` and `Identifier.Invalid`, the inspector is hiding the public string constructor. It exists. Use it - don't try to compute the uint yourself.

## 3. The C# idiom

The full shape. The four identifier names below are **illustrative** - they're the inputs a typical Cartesian-target graph exposes, but the real names come from Section 1.

```csharp
using Hazel;

namespace MyProject
{
    internal class ArmDriver : Entity
    {
        private static readonly Identifier TargetPositionID    = new Identifier("TargetPosition");
        private static readonly Identifier TargetOrientationID = new Identifier("TargetOrientation");
        private static readonly Identifier DurationID          = new Identifier("Duration");
        private static readonly Identifier StartID             = new Identifier("Start");

        private RobotControllerComponent? m_RobotController;
        private MujocoSceneComponent?     m_MujocoScene;
        private MujocoActuator?           m_Gripper;

        protected override void OnCreate()
        {
            m_RobotController = GetComponent<RobotControllerComponent>();
            m_MujocoScene     = GetComponent<MujocoSceneComponent>();
            m_Gripper         = m_MujocoScene?.GetActuator("gripper");
        }

        private void DriveTo(Vector3 worldPos, Vector3 eulerRadians, float seconds)
        {
            if (m_RobotController is null)
                return;

            m_RobotController.SetInputVector3(TargetPositionID,    worldPos);
            m_RobotController.SetInputVector3(TargetOrientationID, eulerRadians * Mathf.Rad2Deg);
            m_RobotController.SetInputFloat  (DurationID,          seconds);
            m_RobotController.SetInputTrigger(StartID);
        }
    }
}
```

Conventions (verify per-graph if the robot differs):

- **Position is world-space (metres), orientation is degrees** for typical Cartesian-target graphs - but units and frame are baked into the graph's input nodes, so a different graph could use a local frame or radians. Confirm by reading the asset if behaviour looks wrong.
- **Convert Euler angles at the boundary, not throughout your code.** The rest of the engine API is radians; multiply by `Mathf.Rad2Deg` only at the `SetInputVector3` call, as shown.
- **`Start` is a trigger, not a bool.** `SetInputTrigger` fires it write-only - there is no `GetInputTrigger`. The graph consumes one trigger event per `SetInputTrigger` call.
- **Each `SetInputTrigger` CANCELS any in-flight motion** and starts a fresh solve toward the most recently written `Target_Position` / `Target_Orientation` / `Duration`. The motion graph is single-target, single-solve - there is NO waypoint queue inside the graph. To sequence N waypoints, fire N triggers spread across N separate frames (or N separate queue steps), with each step's wait >= that motion's duration before the next trigger fires. Calling `SetInputTrigger` twice in the same frame means only the second move runs - the first is overwritten. See `patterns/pick-and-place` Section 2.0a for the queue-step pattern that obeys this rule.
- **Identifiers are `static readonly`.** Constructing them per-call works but the lookup hits an InternalCall every time.
- **Cache components in `OnCreate`.** Don't `GetComponent` every frame.

The setters on `RobotControllerComponent` are `SetInputBool / SetInputInt / SetInputFloat / SetInputVector3 / SetInputTrigger`. Pick the one matching the input's declared type. `GetInputBool / GetInputInt / GetInputFloat / GetInputVector3` read current values back when you need feedback; triggers are write-only.

## 4. Gripper / actuator control

Grippers are MuJoCo actuators, accessed through `MujocoSceneComponent.GetActuator(name)`:

```csharp
m_Gripper.IK    = false;          // mark this actuator as script-owned
m_Gripper.Value = closedValue;    // robot-specific; read from the MJCF
m_Gripper.Value = openValue;
```

- **`.Value` range and direction are MJCF-defined.** Each actuator has its own `ctrlrange` and its own sign convention - one robot may use `[0, 255]` with `0 = closed`, another `[-1, 1]`, another radians for a continuous joint. Read the actuator's `ctrlrange` from the MJCF or ask the user - don't assume. (The C# `MujocoActuator` binding does not expose the range.)
- **`.IK = false` marks the actuator as script-owned.** With `.IK = true` (the default) the motion graph's per-step `RecalculateControls` overwrites the actuator's `ctrl[]` every physics substep, so your `.Value` write gets clobbered. Setting `.IK = false` once in `OnCreate` tells `RecalculateControls` to leave that actuator alone, so subsequent `.Value` writes persist. (Name is historical - the IK-overlay solver itself no longer exists; the flag is now strictly a script-ownership gate.)

## 5. Sequencing motions

There is no built-in "arm reached target" event - the motion graph interpolates over the duration you gave it, and that's it. Sequence multi-step motions by duration:

- Drive `target_1` with duration `d_1`, wait `d_1` seconds, drive `target_2`, etc.
- Use `csharp-api/Timer` (`Timer.Set(callback, seconds)`) or a task-queue helper to do the waiting. See `patterns/timed-behaviors`.
- For branching logic, wrap the queue in a state machine.

## 6. Finding worked examples

If a sibling script in the project already drives the same robot or a similar one, read it first - it'll show the exact input identifier names, gripper actuator name(s), and any sequencing helpers the project has standardised on. `search_assets assetType=ScriptFile` lists the project's script files; `read_file` opens one.

Engine-shipped example projects (under the editor's resource tree, not in `search_assets`) sometimes include complete robot driver scripts. If the user mentions an example or sandbox project by name, ask for its path and `read_file` from there.

## 7. Fallback: no motion graph attached

When the robot root has no `RobotControllerComponent` (or its `MotionGraphAsset` slot is empty), there is no IK and no Cartesian interface. You drive joints by driving actuators directly:

```csharp
var shoulder = m_MujocoScene?.GetActuator("shoulder_pan");
shoulder.Value = controlValue;   // raw MJCF ctrl[]; units defined by the actuator type
```

The full surface for this path on `MujocoSceneComponent`:

- **Discover.** `GetActuator(name)` -> `MujocoActuator?`, `GetActuatorID(name)` -> `int`, `GetJointID(name)` -> `uint`, `GetBodyID(name)` -> `uint`.
- **Read joint state.** `GetJointQposAdr(jointId)` and `GetJointPosition(qposAdr)` for position; `GetJointQvelAdr` + `GetJointVelocity` for velocity. There is no `SetJointPosition` - joint writes go through actuators only.
- **Read body state.** `GetPosition / GetOrientation / GetVelocity / GetAngularVelocity` take a `bodyID` and an optional `hazelSpace` bool.
- **Free-body teleport.** `WeldBody(bodyID, posMj, orientMj, persistent)` for placing free bodies; combined with `GetFreeJointID` / `GetDefaultFreeJointPosition` / `GetDefaultFreeJointQuaternion` for resetting to defaults.

This path bypasses IK - the script is now responsible for inverse kinematics, trajectory shaping, joint limits, and contact-aware planning. Prefer the motion-graph + `LimbIK` route by default. Reach for direct actuator control only when:

- The user explicitly wants joint-space control (e.g. for sysID, RL action spaces, low-level policy outputs).
- The robot has no motion graph and adding one is out of scope.
- A specific actuator should be driven by the script rather than the motion graph - set `actuator.IK = false` to take script ownership (see Section 4).

## End-of-task checklist

Before declaring the task done, mentally verify:

- [ ] `get_entity_properties` confirmed the robot root has `RobotControllerComponent` and `MujocoSceneComponent`.
- [ ] Components are cached in `OnCreate`, not fetched per frame.
- [ ] All Cartesian motion goes through `SetInputVector3 / SetInputFloat / SetInputTrigger` - no `Translation`/`Rotation` writes on robot links.
- [ ] Orientation inputs are converted to degrees at the boundary (`* Mathf.Rad2Deg`).
- [ ] Gripper goes through `MujocoSceneComponent.GetActuator(...).Value`, not parenting or teleportation.
- [ ] Physics-owned objects the robot interacts with stay under physics - the script never writes their `Translation` directly.
- [ ] `build_script_assembly` returned SUCCESS (see `patterns/scripting-workflow` Section 3).
- [ ] The script is attached to an entity with the controller, all `[MUST SET]` fields assigned (`patterns/scripting-workflow` Section 4-5).
- [ ] Summary tells the user what the script does AND to press Play.

See also: `patterns/pick-and-place` (manipulation / stacking on top of the motion-graph layer), `patterns/humanoid-policy-control` (locomotion-policy + arm-IK control for G1 / humanoids), `patterns/scripting-workflow`, `csharp-api/Entity`, `csharp-api/Timer`, `patterns/timed-behaviors`.
